candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest assigns a 0.97 malware probability, and all 20 top n-grams push toward cryptojacking. The evidence is weaker than that suggests. The listed n-grams are generic x86 mnemonic bigrams: stack and calling-convention patterns (SUB PUSH, MOV PUSH, CALL PUSH, PUSH CALL, ADD PUSH, LEA PUSH, POP MOV, MOV LEAVE), plus a few rarer sequences. No function names, API calls, or cryptographic constants are provided, so nothing here can be tied to mining behavior. The high-frequency bigrams (MOV PUSH at 0.0392, ADD PUSH at 0.0337, PUSH CALL at 0.0299, CALL PUSH at 0.0151) are ordinary compiled-code argument setup and call patterns, found in benign and malicious binaries alike. Their SHAP values of about +0.009 to +0.0125 each probably reflect how the model separates its training distribution, not a mining-specific signature. Some low-frequency n-grams are more suggestive but still not definitive. DIV MUL (+0.00694) and FSTP MOV (+0.00655) could reflect arithmetic or floating-point work. CDQ MOV (+0.01445) suggests signed 32-bit division or extension. PUSHFD POP (+0.00914), POP XCHG (+0.00946), POP XOR, POP TEST, POP SUB and CALL RET are unusual stack and flag manipulation, which can appear in obfuscated, packed or hand-written code. LEA MOVSD.REP (+0.00759) suggests block memory copying. These are consistent with obfuscation or unpacking, but they do not show cryptojacking specifically. In short, the model's score is high and the unusual low-frequency sequences hint at obfuscation or arithmetic-heavy code, but the evidence does not show mining-specific behavior such as hashing loops, rotate/shift-heavy rounds or stratum networking. This supports a suspicious-but-inconclusive rating.
